learn.b: Cargo is Rust's build tool and package manager. Run cargo new hello to make a project with a src/main.rs file. Every program starts at fn main.

cargo run builds and runs your program. cargo build only builds it, and cargo check quickly looks for errors without making an executable. Project settings and dependencies live in Cargo.toml, and build output goes in the target folder.
The exclamation mark means println! is a macro, not a normal function. Put {} in the text and Rust fills it with the arguments in order. Use {:?} to print a value in debug form.
You can put a variable name directly inside the braces, like {name}. Comments start with // and run to the end of the line. Lines that are statements end with a semicolon.
learn.code:
let name = "Ana";
println!("Hi {name}"); // greeting

learn.b: let creates a variable that cannot be changed after you set it. Trying to assign a new value is a compile error. This helps prevent accidental bugs.
learn.code:
let x = 5;
// x = 6;  // error

learn.b: Add mut to allow a variable to change. Use it only when you need it. You still keep the same type, so a number stays a number.

const declares a value that never changes and is known at compile time. It always needs a type, and by convention the name is in capital letters. Constants can be declared anywhere, even outside functions.
learn.code: const MAX_POINTS: u32 = 100;

learn.b: You can declare a new variable with the same name using let again. The new one shadows the old one, even in another type. Inside a block the shadow lasts only until the block ends. Shadowing is different from mut because it creates a new variable.

qs.why: You need mut to change them.

learn.b: Use fn, then the name, parameters with types and an arrow with the return type. Rust always needs types on parameters. Functions use snake_case names.
A statement does something and gives no value, like let x = 5;. An expression evaluates to a value, like 5 + 6 or a block in braces. Rust is built from expressions.
The last expression of a function with no semicolon is returned. Adding a semicolon turns it into a statement, so the function returns () instead. Use return to leave early.
Because if is an expression you can assign its result. Both branches must have the same type. A function with no return type returns the unit type ().
learn.code:
let n = if true { 1 } else { 2 };
println!("{n}");

learn.b: The condition must be a bool, Rust never treats numbers as true or false. No parentheses are needed. Use else if for more branches.
loop repeats forever until you break, and break can even return a value. while repeats as long as its condition is true. continue skips to the next round.
for item in collection is the usual loop. A range 1..4 gives 1, 2, 3 and leaves out the end. Write 1..=4 to include 4.
You can loop straight over an array or vector. Labels and break work in nested loops too. The for loop is the safest and most common choice in Rust.

learn.b: Each value in Rust has one owner. There can be only one owner at a time. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory is freed. This is how Rust manages memory without a garbage collector.
String data lives on the heap. When you write let s2 = s1; ownership moves to s2 and s1 can no longer be used. This stops two variables from freeing the same memory.
If you really want two separate values, call clone() to make a deep copy. Simple types like integers, floats, bool and char are Copy, so they are just duplicated and both variables stay valid.

Passing a String to a function moves it into the function, and it is dropped when the function ends. The function can give ownership back by returning the value. Next you will learn borrowing, which avoids this.

learn.b: A reference lets you use a value without taking ownership. Write &s to borrow s. The function that receives it has the parameter type &String, and the owner keeps the value afterwards.
Use &mut to borrow in a way that lets the function change the value. The variable itself must be declared mut. Use * to reach the value behind a reference.

At any moment you can have either many shared references & or exactly one &mut, never both at once. References must always be valid. These rules, checked by the borrow checker, prevent data races and dangling pointers.
A slice borrows part of a collection. For text, &s[0..5] is a string slice of type &str. String literals are also &str. Slices do not own their data.

learn.b: A struct bundles named fields. Create an instance with every field filled in. Read fields with a dot, and make the instance mut to change them.
An impl block holds the methods for a type. The first parameter is &self to read, &mut self to change, or self to take ownership. Call methods with a dot.

A function in impl without self is an associated function, called with Type::name(). The usual one is new, which acts like a constructor. Self means the type being implemented. If the parameter has the same name as a field, you can write the field shorthand.
Add #[derive(Debug)] above a struct to print it with {:?}. A tuple struct has unnamed fields, like struct Meters(f64). These make types that mean something specific.

learn.b: An enum lists the possible values of a type, called variants. Variants can hold data too, so one enum can describe several shapes of information.
match compares a value against patterns and runs the first one that fits. It must be exhaustive, covering every case. Use _ as a catch-all.
Rust has no null. Option<T> is either Some(value) or None. You must handle both, so you cannot forget a missing value. if let is a short way to handle just one pattern.

Result<T, E> is either Ok(value) or Err(error), used for things that can fail. Match on it, or use unwrap and expect which panic on failure, expect with your own message. The ? operator returns the error early from the function.

learn.b: A Vec<T> is a growable list. Make one with vec![1, 2, 3] or Vec::new(). Use push to add, pop to remove the last item, and v.get(i) to get an Option instead of risking a crash. Loop with for x in &v.

String is an owned, growable piece of text, while &str is a borrowed slice. Use String::from or to_string to make one, push_str to add text, and format! to build text without printing. len counts bytes.
A HashMap stores key and value pairs. Bring it in with use std::collections::HashMap;. insert adds, get returns an Option, and entry().or_insert() sets a default if the key is missing.

A trait describes shared behavior as method signatures. A type opts in with impl Trait for Type. Generic functions can require a trait with a bound like T: Summary. Traits can also have default methods.
